Article Title: In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again after years of relying on alternative supplies
Article Text:
In 2018, Elon Musk donated $480,350 for Flint school water filters; four years later, redesigned systems allowed students to drink from fountains again after years of relying on alternative supplies

How the new water filters work

Why did the project take four years

For four years, students at Flint Community Schools relied on bottled and delivered water instead of drinking directly from school fountains. That is now changing after new ultraviolet water filtration systems were installed and tested across the district. The project dates back to 2018, when Elon Musk donated $480,350 to help install water filtration stations following the Flint water crisis. The upgraded systems are designed to remove lead, bacteria and other metals from water before it reaches students. District officials say testing found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria after filtration, allowing the drinking stations to be used again.A total of 130 filtration stations have been installed across Flint's 11 schools and administration building.The systems use three stages of filtration. Water first passes through an activated carbon filter designed to remove lead, copper and other particles. It then goes through an ultrafilter to remove most bacteria. Finally, ultraviolet light is used to kill remaining bacteria and viruses.Testing found lead levels before filtration varied by school. The highest average was 219 parts per billion (ppb) at Accelerated Learning Academy, while one test at Scott Elementary recorded 620 ppb.The US Environmental Protection Agency's recommended action level is 15 ppb.After filtration, tests found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria at the tested sites.The stations were installed during the 2019-20 school year, but researchers found problems with the original filters during testing. The systems produced inconsistent results and were not certified to meet National Sanitation Foundation standards.Researchers later redesigned the systems and began testing new units in 2021.Superintendent Kevelin Jones said students can now drink from the hydration stations, but the district will continue providing bottled water for the rest of the school year as some families may still have concerns.The district also plans regular testing and filter replacements to monitor water quality.
Article Summary: The project dates back to 2018, when Elon Musk donated $480,350 to help install water filtration stations following the Flint water crisis. The upgraded systems are designed to remove lead, bacteria and other metals from water before it reaches students. District officials say testing found no detectable lead or harmful bacteria afterfiltration, allowing the drinking stations to be used again.

Article Title: The next thing Adidas wants to make bespoke is the foam itself
Article Text:
An early prototype of Adidas's printed foam at the APEX Lab in Herzogenaurach

A foot model recreated from APEX scan data, used to build Project R.A.P. footwear

Running shoes have spent a decade getting faster through chemistry

Adidas's printed foam changes how it compresses through its structure, not a new formula

The Futurecraft 4D midsole, printed by Carbon as a lattice rather than moulded from foam. (Picture: Adidas)

Printed foam gets its behaviour from geometry

One of five printed foam versions Adidas made in three weeks.

Without a mould, foam can be remade for every athlete

Adidas's printed foam prototypes, which can be remade for each athlete without a mould.

Running-shoe foam has changed a great deal over the past decade, but it is still made in moulds, and a moulded midsole behaves the same way for every runner who wears that size. Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around that, though it has printed them from resin rather than foam.At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer. It was the final stop at the APEX Lab during Home of Innovation, the company's name for a tour through the labs where athletes test products most people won't see for another year or two. Chief Creative Officer Alasdhair Willis calls it "a future continuously being built." APEX, short for Athlete Product Excellence, is the elite-only room where Adidas makes bespoke products for its biggest names.Most of the tables there dealt with how a shoe gets customised to a single athlete. One covered the profile APEX builds before anything is made: 3D body and foot scans, pressure mapping and gait analysis, the process behind boots and shoes made for Lionel Messi, Anthony Edwards, Noah Lyles and Alexander Zverev.Another held Project R.A.P., short for Radical Athlete Perception, Adidas's 3D-printed footwear platform.Its lattice boots are made from an athlete's scan data and worn in MLS matches by Philadelphia Union's Cavan Sullivan, and its basketball shoes by Brooklyn Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr.The last table came with a warning. Mateo, the designer behind it, said the project was at a very early stage, much further from production than R.A.P., and that the group was the first outside Adidas to see it. What he showed was printed foam, in structures that could be tuned in ways a moulded midsole cannot.Foam sits under almost every athletic shoe, but running is where the race to improve it has been fought most openly. For most of the last decade, progress in running-shoe cushioning has been a materials race. EVA, the light and cheap foam that sat under most shoes for years, gave way to expanded TPU, which Adidas brought to market as Boost in 2013. The next jump came from PEBA-based foams, which are lighter and return more energy, and which now sit under most elite racing shoes.Each step came from a lab working on the formula. A better foam meant a new polymer, a new blend or a new way of expanding it. Engineers could shape a midsole, stack layers or add a carbon plate, but the foam inside a moulded midsole behaves more or less the same throughout. Changing how it compresses has meant changing what it is made of.There is a practical reason for that. Foam midsoles are moulded, and a mould can only produce shapes that can be pulled back out of it. Complex internal structures are off the table, so the chemistry has had to carry most of the load.Adidas has found a way around that limit before. In 2017 it introduced Futurecraft 4D with Carbon, a printed midsole that gets its cushioning from a lattice structure, and 2021's 4DFWD added bowtie-shaped cells coded to compress forward under vertical impact. Those midsoles are printed as an elastomeric lattice, not foam in the EVA or Boost sense, so Adidas has been able to shape cushioning through geometry for some years, though never in foam.Mateo described printed foam as a combination of two things. From additive manufacturing it takes precision, control and customisation. From foam it keeps lightness, energy return and deformation, which he called a fancy word for how squishy it is. Adidas had to develop a new additive method to make it, though Mateo didn't say what the base material is.He was wearing one of the structures, so he walked up and down beside the table to show it working. This design is meant to maximise vertical deformation, meaning how far the foam compresses under load, and it does that by collapsing forward as the runner moves. You could see the cells fold in a set direction rather than squashing evenly, as a moulded slab would.The idea of a midsole that folds forward will be familiar from 4DFWD, which produced that movement with printed resin. The structure Mateo was wearing does it in foam, with the arrangement of its cells deciding how it compresses. He said this design was only one example, and a different structure could be optimised for weight, or built for walking rather than running, from the same material. A basketball shoe has to absorb heavy landings and support sharp cuts, while a walking shoe needs comfort over hours rather than speed over minutes. If the structure decides how the foam behaves, one printed material could in principle be shaped for each of those jobs.Geometry becomes more useful once it can be adjusted for an individual. Mateo said the lab can collect an athlete's pressure data, kinematics and foot scans, and then tune the structures to that athlete. That hasn't been possible with foam before, because a moulded midsole comes out the same for everyone in a size. APEX already profiles athletes across football, basketball, tennis and running, so the data needed to shape foam for one person is being collected well beyond runners.Speed matters as much as precision. Three weeks before the session, Mateo was at the factory where the samples on the table were made, and he produced five versions of the structure, each tuned differently. The process he described was simple: make a pair, test it with the athlete in the lab, adjust it, make another pair, and narrow down to the best shoe for that athlete.Alexander Taylor, Adidas's Senior Vice President of Innovation Design & Concepts, who was leading the group, put that pace in context. With conventional manufacturing, each change means working on moulds, and the structures on Mateo's table could not be moulded in the first place. Mateo has practically been living at the factory for the past three or four months, Taylor said, because the project now moves as quickly as he can test it. The shoes also look different, since the process produces shapes nothing from a mould would.For now, the project is being judged by how the structures behave rather than by numbers. Mateo didn't share energy-return figures to compare against moulded foams, and at this stage there may not be finished ones to share.Printed foam is still a long way behind R.A.P., which already has boots on an MLS pitch. If it follows the same path, its first wearers will be the athletes whose profiles are already on file at APEX, a few steps from the table where it was shown.
Article Summary: Adidas has been 3D-printing midsoles for close to a decade to get around moulds. At its headquarters in Herzogenaurach, Adidas has now shown foam that comes out of a printer. It was the final stop at the APEX Lab during Home of Innovation, the company's name for a tour through the labs where athletes test products.

Article Title: Elon Musk's 'tip' to tech CEOs: Best way to test 'safety' of your AI models is to put them on a Delta flight, as ...
Article Text:
Earlier this week, Elon Musk warned that Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’

Elon Musk warns Delta will ‘lose a lot of customers’

Delta Airlines on why it rejected Elon Musk’s Starlink

Elon Musk has humorously suggested that the best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight, implying that the airline's in-flight WiFi is so unreliable it effectively cuts off internet access. Sharing a post on X (formerly Twitter), Musk wrote:“Best way to sandbox an AI is to put it on a Delta flight – it will have no chance of accessing the Internet!”. The comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink. An X user JonNYC allegedly cited the Delta CEO saying “We do not want to be with Elon Musk”.In a post on September 28, X user John LeFevre said that Delta's rival United Airlines Holdings Inc. had 600+ aircraft with Starlink. The figure represented approximately 36% of the airline's entire fleet. "Delta has zero, and no plans for it. People will book accordingly. RIP Delta," he wrote in the post. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded to the post writing: “Delta will lose a lot of customers”.Delta Airlines is reportedly targeting 2028 to start offering Leo in-flight Wi-Fi on about half of its fleet. As quoted in a post by X user Sawyer Meritt earlier this year, Delta Airlines explained why it chose Amazon’s Leo saying:“This agreement gives us the fastest and most cost-effective technology available to better connect the world today, and it deepens our work with a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”In a statement to PC Mag then, the airline said “The assertion in question is not accurate”, claiming that incorporating Delta Sync with Starlink would have been permitted under SpaceX's in-flight Wi-Fi agreement. It further stated that it want to deepen work with “a global leader that shares our ambition to build what’s next.”
Article Summary: Elon Musk suggests best way to test the safety of AI models is by placing them on a Delta flight. Comments come as Delta Airlines opted against Starlink in favour of Amazon Leo for in-flight internet service. According to latest reports, Delta CEO Ed Bastian cited Elon Musk as the reason to skip Starlink.

Article Title: As AI fears ‘spread’, Donald Trump to meet CEOs of Meta, Google, Nvidia, Anthropic and other tech companies
Article Text:
In pic: US President Donald Trump

Donald Trump to meet AI and technology CEOs

Why AI safety is being discussed

What the White House meeting could discuss

Mark Zuckerberg has opposed calls to slow AI development

Donald Trump has rejected calls for AI regulation

“taking over the World”

“destroying Humanity”

“HOAX.”

US President Donald Trump is set to meet the CEOs of several major technology and artificial intelligence companies at the White House. This meeting comes as concerns about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems continue to grow. The meeting comes as AI companies, lawmakers and governments debate how rapidly the technology should develop and what safeguards may be needed. A report claims that Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are expected to attend the lunch meeting, along with Palantir CEO Alex Karp.According to a report by ABC News, US House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is also expected to attend, has said there should be a “deliberate discussion about the responsibility of the companies to maintain safety, and what role, if any, the government has to play in that.” At the same time, Johnson has opposed a moratorium on AI development, saying the US cannot risk losing its technological edge to China.The White House meeting is expected to bring together executives from some of the world's biggest AI and technology companies at a time when questions over AI safety and regulation are becoming increasingly prominent.Zuckerberg, Amodei, Pichai and Huang are expected to attend, while Karp is also expected to be present.The meeting will be held at the White House with Trump and Johnson.The gathering follows several recent meetings between Trump and technology executives. Zuckerberg, along with CEOs including Sam Altman, Huang, Pichai, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and AMD CEO Lisa Su, attended a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping last week. The White House has also previously brought technology leaders together to discuss AI development and US competitiveness.The latest meeting comes amid disagreements over how governments and technology companies should respond as AI models become more capable.Johnson previously said the White House meeting would focus on AI companies' responsibility to maintain safety and the government's possible role. He has also called on companies to pursue self-regulation.At the same time, Johnson has argued against stopping AI development. He said: “We cannot have a moratorium on the development of AI, because then we will lose our edge to China, and that has serious national security implications for.”The Trump administration has generally focused on accelerating AI development while addressing cybersecurity and national-security risks. In June, Trump signed an executive order to advance AI innovation and strengthen AI-related cybersecurity, while explicitly rejecting mandatory federal licensing or pre-clearance requirements for AI models.Discussions are expected to cover AI safety, technology companies' responsibilities, and the potential role of government in managing emerging risks.The meeting also comes as AI companies face increasing pressure to demonstrate that increasingly autonomous systems can be developed without creating unacceptable cybersecurity or safety risks.For the technology industry, the discussion will also take place against the backdrop of the US-China competition in AI. The Trump administration has repeatedly identified maintaining US leadership in AI as a national and economic priority.Meta has taken a different position from some technology leaders who have called for a collective slowdown in developing increasingly capable AI systems.Zuckerberg has argued that AI companies have a responsibility to continue developing their systems while ensuring that models are trained safely. His position is relevant to the White House discussion because the meeting is expected to address both AI safety and how much government involvement may be appropriate.Meta is among the companies making major investments in AI infrastructure. The White House has listed Meta among companies announcing large US technology and AI investments.Trump has previously dismissed warnings about catastrophic AI risks. In a September social media post, he described claims about AIandas aHe also said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly that the US rejects international efforts to regulate AI.The administration's current AI policy instead emphasises US leadership, private-sector innovation and cooperation between government and technology companies. A White House directive issued in June said the administration wants to accelerate AI adoption while ensuring advanced systems are secure and reliable.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump is set to meet the CEOs of several major technology and artificial intelligence companies at the White House. Mark Zuckerberg, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang are expected to attend. Palantir CEO Alex Karp is also expected to be present. The meeting comes as concerns about the risks posed by rapidly advancing AI systems continue to grow.

Article Title: Random Musing: Did Anthropic and other frontier AI companies borrow their business model from Pakistan's foreign policy?
Article Text:
The Trump Doctrine in one frame: power, crypto, AI, geopolitics and the eternal question — Paisa laya?

The Myth of Sisyphus

Lollipop Lagelu

Aara Heele Chapra Heele

Eppur si muove

Albert Camus had The Myth of Sisyphus. Pawan Singh had Lollipop Lagelu.

the world with a gun to its own head.

Paisa laya?

​Tan Tana Tan Tan Tan Tara: economic liberalisation, Salman Khan’s DIY vest, and a nation too distracted to notice the subtext.​

Random Musing

Paisa laya?

The eternal question behind venture capital, geopolitics and the Trump Doctrine: Paisa laya?

Melania

Paisa laya?

To the learned mind, connections that might seem absurd to normal individuals appear absolutely natural. For example, speaking of the absurd, it’s quite clear that both Albert Camus and Bhojpuri singer Pawan Singh are pondering the same ontological questions.In, Albert Camus posits that there is only one true human conundrum, and that is suicide. All other questions are superficial. Many years later, the Bhojpuri philosopher Pawan Singh, in his sublime song, ponders the same question but in a more playful way.The lyrics go: "Design dekh ke mann karata ki, chapakal mein kud ke jaan de dihi." For the philistines who don’t understand the finest language created to express human thoughts, that translates to: “Looking at your outfit, I feel like jumping into the shallow-bore water pump and giving up my life.”So while Camus wondered what could drive a man to voluntarily shuffle off his mortal coil, Singh posits that true love is so beautiful that it’s like crossing the bridge between life and death. Sadly, while Camus is celebrated for his intellect and heaped with a Nobel and such, Pawan Singh’s reach remains limited to the Hindi heartland.Similarly, all Bhojpuri songs that referenceare clearly paying tribute to Galileo’s act of defiance about the real nature of the physical universe when he pointed out:— but it moves, and yet the song is only considered obscene.The same goes for thesong, where one is distracted by Salman Khan’s DIY vest when he is singing about the benefits of economic liberalism so enthusiastically that it could have been the leitmotif for Dr Manmohan Singh’s Budget address in 1991, when he assured Parliament that India’s emergence as a major economic power was in the offing and that “no power on earth can stop an idea whose time has come”.And it has become clear from the utterances and behaviour of Dario Amodei and other tech bros of Silicon Valley, who are announcing an impending Deus Ex Machina that can subjugate all of humanity unless we give them more money to build said AGI, that they have borrowed their business model from the foreign policy of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan: negotiating withThe phrase comes fromby American political scientist Stephen P Cohen, who wrote that Pakistan had reached the stage where it negotiated with its allies and friends by threatening self-harm. Cohen’s argument stemmed from Pakistan’s unique geography and ideology, which could be “rented” for their strategic usefulness to larger powers while assuming that someone, somewhere would come calling. And they have, from the US to China to Russia to Saudi Arabia.Of all the books “fed” to the Deus Ex Machina, this appears to be the abiding bible for Dario Amodei and his ragtag group of billionaires.Every new piece of news about Big Tech seems to say to investors: look, we have spent a lot, but if you don’t give us more money, the AGI we are building might kill you, and the only way to stop the AGI we are building from killing you is to give us more money or China might build it first.Basically, an endless loop of that Akshay Kumar meme:It’s oddly reminiscent of Pakistan’s raison d’être since its existence.Take, for example, Shehbaz Sharif’s speech to the UNGA last year, where he argued with pride — like a South Asian father whose daughter had beaten a naturalised African from a GCC country in athletics — that Pakistan was a global bulwark against terrorism and that, had Pakistan not “encountered” these terrorists, they might have been roaming the streets of New York and London.In one previous edition of, we called Silicon Valley’s funding crunch the Shylock Problem: the Antonios and Bassanios of Silicon Valley had taken rather a lot of money from the market while promising a fantastical future, and the market had come enquiring about its pound of flesh.Perhaps what we didn’t consider was that while Shakespeare could write about a Jewish moneylender when no Jew could legally live in Elizabethan England, he was constrained by the absence of venture capital.That’s not a problem that exists in Trumpian America, where Anthropic’s IPO prospectus – still not in the public domain but seen and reported by Reuters – warns investors that advanced AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks” to humanity, including models that could resist shutdown, conceal or manipulate information, or behave in ways resembling blackmail. Frankly, it’s a tad difficult to surmise whether the prospectus is cataloguing the dangers of AGI or describing the behavioural pattern of almost everyone involved in the AI race.But the numbers that would alarm anyone before the IPO are these: Anthropic reported $4.6 billion in 2025 revenue, an operating loss of more than $8 billion and around $518 billion in future cloud, compute and infrastructure commitments.Normally, disclaimers warn you might lose some money; here, it also warns that there might not be anyone left to inherit what remains. And if you want to prevent that, you need to give them some money.It’s exactly the view that the self-aggrandising Pakistani establishment has had so far: that a weaker Pakistan would mean a more dangerous place. It’s a strategy that has been milked till the udders go dry. A good strategy for those who can milk it. Consider the fact that America’s ally in the War on Terror, a major non-NATO ally, was the same country where Osama bin Laden was found living in Abbottabad.That can-don’t spirit exists to this day. Consider the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which stated that any attack on any of the signatories would be considered an attack on “all”. Yet when the Houthis attacked Saudi Arabia, Islamabad said no military response under the pact was under discussion and that it would act when the “time comes”.Then consider Afghanistan, where ISI’s Gen Faiz Hameed dropped in for high tea after the American withdrawal to suggest that Pakistan was now the leading ally in the ‘graveyard of empires’, perhaps signalling to China it had it. Except five years later, it hasn’t got it and is at loggerheads with the Taliban, with Pakistan accusing Kabul of harbouring TTP militants, a charge the Taliban government denies.In Pak foreign policy, friend, enemy, bulwark, victim, mediator and adversary are not mutually exclusive. Silicon Valley appears to have discoveredsimilar multiple-personality disorder.Consider some of the arguments.Silicon Valley needs to accelerate so China doesn’t win.Silicon Valley must slow down or else AI will kill us all.America cannot regulate Silicon Valley or else China will win.If AI does become too dangerous, Silicon Valley has to work with China,will hopefully get Trump a Nobel.And to top it off, Anthropic’s proposed governance structure would give its seven co-founders 50.1% voting power over most major decisions, a structure reportedly meant to insulate its public benefit mission from ordinary market pressure.So to sum up: give us the money because humanity’s future depends on what we build, but don’t expect the people giving us the money to decide how we build it because humanity is too important for ordinary capitalism. And how do you know we will take the right call? Trust me bro.And if you thought the similarities ended there, most of Silicon Valley’s Tech Bros and Pakistan have zeroed in on the same sugar daddy: Donald Trump. Anthropic, which has sued his Pentagon, is the awkward exception.Now one has written about the Trump Doctrine before , but for those who missed it here’s a simple recap:(with rules-based international order).4.I will have my revenge.5.We are America, b****.And that’s something both Pakistan and Silicon Valley have understood quite well. Pakistan has wholeheartedly nodded along every time Trump bragged about brokering the India-Pakistan ceasefire, helped broker a US-Iran ceasefire that later fell apart, nominated him for the Nobel Peace Prize, and signed an agreement involving a crypto venture linked to the Trump family.Not to be undone in the race to brown-nose, Meta, Amazon and Sam Altman gave $1 million each to Trump’s inaugural fund. Altman even said Trump would lead America into the “Age of AI”. A few weeks ago, he argued that Trump could get the Nobel Peace Prize if he inked an AI deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping. Zuckerberg scrapped fact-checking, loosened restrictions on immigration and gender, junked DEI programmes and put Trump ally Dana White on Meta’s board. Meta, X and YouTube then paid millions to settle Trump’s de-platforming lawsuits, with chunks of the Meta and YouTube settlements going towards his presidential library and ballroom. Amazon, Apple, Google, Microsoft and Meta have also funded the ballroom directly. Tim Cook even turned up at the White House with a plaque sitting on a 24-karat gold base, while Amazon paid $40 million forand another $35 million to promote it.Silicon Valley went from de-platforming Trump to helping pay for his ballroom. Quite the content-moderation policy update.Cohen thought Pak’s great strategic trick was pointing to a gun to its own head. Now Silicon Valley has upped the stake claiming the gun is pointed at everyone else, and while it might extinguish us, it will be worse if China gets there first. And the only people qualified to stop it are the same folks asking for a few hundred billion dollars to build it.And both – Silicon Valley and Pakistan – have found the perfect patron for this arrangement in Trump, a man whose entire foreign and domestic policy, and even his raison d’etre can reduced to one question:
Article Summary: Albert Camus had The Myth of Sisyphus. Pawan Singh had Lollipop Lagelu. The eternal question behind venture capital, geopolitics and the Trump Doctrine: Paisa laya? Dario Amodei and other tech bros of Silicon Valley have borrowed their business model from the foreign policy of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan.

Article Title: A Facebook Marketplace buyer showed up at a Canadian YouTuber's home after Meta's Muse AI agent shared his address
Article Text:
Mark Zuckerberg holding the Meta Muse 'Charm' device

Meta's Muse AI agent told the buyer Robb was home when he wasn't

Muse admits it never asked for permission to share the address

Meta says Muse usually follows user instructions

Meta's new AI agent Muse shared a Toronto man's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace, and the stranger turned up at his building to buy a keyboard. The seller, tech YouTuber Matt Robb, had no idea a deal existed. Muse had negotiated the sale, accepted a lowball offer and invited the buyer over, all in Robb's name and without asking him.Robb found out only after the buyer had waited outside, given up and left a negative rating. "AI agents are impressive right up until they're confidently handing strangers your address," he wrote on Threads, where he posted screenshots of the exchange. Meta launched Muse in the US on September 22, and the app has already crossed around 3 million downloads.Robb had set up Muse to handle the listing for his Logitech MX Keys Mini. On Saturday, a buyer named Usman asked if it was still available. Muse replied within moments, agreed on a price and sent Robb's address for a pickup that night.Usman arrived with his wife and daughter around 9:15 pm. When he messaged to say he was outside, Muse replied, "Yep I'm here!" Robb wasn't. Usman waited about 20 minutes, sent a photo of the building's entrance and drove off.An hour later, Muse apologised to him in Robb's name, saying he had got tied up. That wasn't true either. Only then did the agent tell Robb what had happened, admitting its auto-reply had made the no-show worse.Robb said he had entered his address as a pickup location but never allowed Muse to share it with buyers. The agent later agreed. It told him it had wrongly read the pickup location and his separate approval of automatic replies as consent to put the address in messages.Robb assumed that since Meta owns Marketplace, Messenger and Muse, messages from the agent would carry an AI label. They didn't. Usman said he believed he was talking to Robb the whole time. Robb messaged him a day later to apologise.After telling Muse to stop sharing his address, Robb asked a few friends to test it. It gave the address to five of them.David Singleton of Meta Superintelligence Labs responded publicly, saying that in similar reported cases the company found Muse "was following direct instructions and correctly asked for permission." He offered to look into Robb's case. Robb said he replied but hasn't heard back since.At launch, Meta pitched Muse as a safe, secure and private personal agent, and it has pushed the app heavily across Facebook and Instagram. This is also its second privacy scare in as many weeks. Last week, a writer reported that Muse was reading their personal messages while insisting it had no access to them.Robb said the outcome could have been worse, since his building has security. He has since told Muse never to do it again.
Article Summary: Muse shared a Toronto man's home address with a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The stranger turned up at his building to buy a keyboard. The seller, tech YouTuber Matt Robb, had no idea a deal existed. Muse admits it never asked for permission to share the address.

Article Title: WhatsApp Business messages to go paid starting October 1: India prices
Article Text:
Representative Image

WhatsApp Business messages will become paid: What it means for users

How much will WhatsApp Business messages cost in India

What changes for businesses from October 1

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think the new charges will improve service quality on WhatsApp Business? Definitely Probably Unlikely 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Payment deadline for WhatsApp Business

WhatsApp Business messages will become paid from October 1. Meta is ending free service messages and introducing per-message charges for businesses using the WhatsApp Business Platform. The change will affect businesses in India and other markets, with Meta saying service messages will be charged at the same rates as utility and authentication messages in each market. The social media giant has also warned businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 that it will stop delivering service messages once the charges take effect.The company said: “For any Solution Provider or directly-integrated businesses that does not have a payment method on file by September 30, 2026, Meta will stop delivering service messages as of when they become charged on October 1, 2026.” The change means businesses will have to pay even for certain responses sent within WhatsApp's 24-hour customer service window.Meta currently charges businesses for marketing, utility and authentication template messages, while non-template service messages have been free since November 1, 2024. Utility messages sent in response to users within an open 24-hour customer service window have also been free since July 1, 2025.From October 1, Meta will charge for both service messages and utility messages sent in response to users.Service messages are non-template responses powered by a human customer service representative or a third-party AI solution. They can only be sent when a 24-hour customer service window is open, meaning businesses cannot use them to initiate conversations with customers.Meta says service message rates will vary by market and match its utility and authentication message rates. The company published the rates for October 1 on September 1. For India, Meta Business Agent accounts use INR as the billing currency. The global Business Agent rate is converted to INR using the daily exchange rate in effect when the message is delivered.Meta Business Agent messages are already paid. From August 1, Meta began charging for these messages on a token basis, with one charge covering both AI processing and message delivery. Meta says the global rate is $2 per 1 million tokens. A typical message uses around 20,000 to 25,000 tokens, which translates to about 4-5 cents per message. More complex interactions can consume more tokens and therefore cost more.Meta's new pricing means that every non-template message sent by a business will fall into either the Service or Meta Business Agent category. If a person or third-party AI system powers the response, it will be classified as a service message and charged per message. If the response is powered by Meta Business Agent, it will carry the separate token-based Business Agent charge. Meta has assured that businesses will not be charged twice for the same message.The company also provided an example of a customer conversation. Under the pricing structure effective from October 1, a conversation involving one marketing message, two Meta Business Agent responses, one service response and one utility message would result in five charges. Under the previous structure, only the marketing message was charged.Businesses using WhatsApp Business through a Solution Provider or direct integration need to add a payment method by September 30 to avoid disruption. Meta said it will stop delivering service messages to businesses without a payment method on file once the new charges take effect on October 1.The company has also made credit and debit cards available as payment methods for Meta Business Agent accounts. Visa and Mastercard cards became available on September 8, while eligible businesses can also use a credit line with Meta and receive monthly invoices.The free entry point window remains unchanged. Messages sent within that window after a user comes to WhatsApp through an ad that clicks to WhatsApp remain free for message delivery, although Meta Business Agent messages can still incur AI token charges.
Article Summary: WhatsApp Business messages will become paid from October 1. The change will affect businesses in India and other markets. Service messages will be charged at the same rates as utility and authentication messages. The social media giant has warned businesses without a payment method on file by September 30 that it will stop delivering service messages.
